title: Ascra Under Helicon: the Shepherd Given a Voice and the Bones Carried to Orchomenus
years: fl. c. 700 BC (conventional range c. 750-650 BC)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cyme in Aeolis, the father takes ship
stops.date_confidence: No date survives. Works and Days 633-640 gives the migration no year and sets it before the poem's present; the year here only opens the sequence. Hesiod's floruit is conventionally c. 700 BCE with a scholarly range of c. 750-650 BCE (Britannica), while Herodotus 2.53 places him four hundred years before his own time, which points to the mid-ninth century instead. The two estimates are left standing against each other.
stops.campa: A man leaves the Aeolian port of Cyme on the Anatolian coast because he cannot make a living in it. His son will say so in a poem, generations of shipping compressed into one line: he fled not riches but wretched poverty, the kind Zeus lays on men. The father takes ship across the Aegean with whatever a poor household carries. He is never named in the poems that record him. Later writers call him Dios and his wife Pycimede, on no authority earlier than the Byzantine lexicons and the scholia. What trade he followed at Cyme, no source says.
stops.quote: One day he came to this very place crossing over a great stretch of sea; he left Aeolian Cyme and fled, not from riches and substance, but from wretched poverty which Zeus lays upon men, and he settled near Helicon in a miserable hamlet, Ascra, which is bad in winter, sultry in summer, and good at no time.
stops.quote_source: Hesiod, Works and Days 633-640, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348
suggested_refs: The harbour of Aeolian Cyme, port of the family's departure
The Suda and the scholia, sole sources for the names Dios and Pycimede
sources: Hesiod, Works and Days 633-640 (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: Ascra, the hamlet good at no time
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The settlement precedes the poem's present by an unstated interval; the year orders the segment only. Coordinates follow the Wikipedia site entry for Ascra (38.327032, 23.074249). Flagged: those coordinates sit roughly 22 km east of Wikipedia's own coordinates for Mount Helicon (38.35278, 22.82250), an inconsistency in the reference sources that this file records rather than resolves.
stops.campa: The father settles inland, under the mountain, in a village called Ascra. It has no harbour and no fleet, and its weather earns the only description of it that survives from a man who lived there: bad in winter, sultry in summer, good at no time. A Greek from an Anatolian port becomes a Boeotian smallholder, and his sons will inherit ploughland rather than a berth. Whether the poet was born here or carried here as a child from Cyme, the poems do not say, and no ancient writer settles it.
suggested_refs: The site of Ascra on the lower slopes of Helicon, in Thespian territory
sources: Hesiod, Works and Days 639-640 (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: Ascra, the oxen and the hired hands
stops.date_confidence: Undated; the year orders the segment. Works and Days describes a working household in detail but supplies no year, no acreage, and no statement of what Hesiod himself owned. Direct textual fact about the world the poem depicts, not evidence of the poet's own station.
stops.campa: The farm the poem teaches is fully stocked: a plough and a spare, a yoke of nine-year-old oxen, mules, seed, jars, a hired man, a hired woman, slaves. None of this is offered as an inventory of Hesiod's own holding; it is the working standard of a Boeotian household, and the poem assumes throughout that one man commands it. The instruction runs to the practical extreme. Buy a servant woman who has no child, it says, so that no infant takes her hours.
suggested_refs: The household-management passages of Works and Days as evidence for early Greek rural slaveholding
sources: Hesiod, Works and Days, household passages (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: Mount Helicon, the lambs and the goddesses
stops.date_confidence: Undated and not verifiable as biography. Theogony 22-34 is a first-person commissioning scene and is treated here as tradition rather than event; the research pool tagged the same episode both ways and the defensible tag is tradition. The text gives no age for him. Coordinates are Wikipedia's for Mount Helicon (38.35278, 22.82250); the exact pasture has no landmark.
stops.campa: He is pasturing lambs on the mountain above his village when the Muses come to him. They open with an insult: shepherds of the wilderness, wretched things of shame, mere bellies. Then they say the thing every later Greek poet will have to answer, that they know how to speak many false things as though they were true, and know also, when they will, to utter true things. They breathe a divine voice into him and tell him to sing. The poem does not say how old he is.
stops.quote: Shepherds of the wilderness, wretched things of shame, mere bellies, we know how to speak many false things as though they were true; but we know, when we will, to utter true things.
stops.quote_source: Hesiod, Theogony 26-28, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348
suggested_refs: The slopes of Helicon above Ascra, scene of the commissioning in Theogony 22-34

stops.name: Mount Helicon, the staff of flowering laurel
stops.date_confidence: Undated; same scene as the preceding stop, separated only to hold the textual problem. The Greek of Theogony 30 reads skeptron daphnes erithaleos ozon, and daphne is laurel. Flagged: the Evelyn-White translation used for the quotes in this file renders the same line as a shoot of sturdy olive, so the laurel reading rests on the Greek and on Pausanias 9.30.3, not on Evelyn-White.
stops.campa: They give him a staff. The Greek at Theogony 30 is daphne, laurel, a branch of it in flower, and the staff is the whole of his equipment: no lyre, no strings, nothing to play. He is told to sing what will be and what was before, and to begin and end with the Muses themselves. A poet who holds a stick rather than an instrument is a different kind of performer from the singers of the Homeric tradition, and the difference will later cost him an entry at Delphi. Evelyn-White's English, the version most readers meet, prints an olive shoot in that line.
suggested_refs: Pausanias 9.30.3, which objects that the statue of Hesiod on Helicon holds a harp although his own verses give him a laurel wand
sources: Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.30.3 (Jones, via Wikisource Book 9)
Hesiod, Theogony, trans. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348, for the divergent rendering

stops.name: The Valley of the Muses, the sanctuary below the peak
stops.date_confidence: Coordinates approximate: the exact ancient Mouseion within the Valley of the Muses near Thespiae could not be pinned to a landmark-level source in this pass. Flagged: Thespian administration of the sanctuary is standard scholarship but was not confirmed from the cited Wikipedia article on Thespiae, which describes instead a quinquennial festival of Eros, the Erotidia, held in the Helicon grove with contests in music and athletics.
stops.campa: Below the peak, in the hollow the Thespians hold, lies the ground sacred to the Muses: a grove, springs, and in time an altar and a festival with contests in music and in athletics. Hesiod's poems name the goddesses of Helicon over and over and give this valley its authority; the sanctuary's own buildings, so far as archaeology can date them, belong to the classical and Hellenistic centuries, long after him. What stood here while he was alive is not known.
suggested_refs: The Valley of the Muses below Helicon, in the territory of Thespiae

stops.name: Ascra, the name that sends forth the voice
stops.date_confidence: Interpretive, not biographical. The self-naming at Theogony 22 is attested in the text. The etymology is Gregory Nagy's published reading and could not be verified against a primary Nagy text in this pass; it is recorded as an attributed scholarly claim. The date only orders the segment.
stops.campa: He puts his own name into the Theogony in the third person: they taught Hesiod glorious song while he was shepherding his lambs under holy Helicon. No other early Greek poet signs himself so plainly inside the work, and the Homeric poems name no author at all. What his parents called him is recorded nowhere. Gregory Nagy reads the name as a programme rather than a birth-name, hienai and aude, he who sends forth the voice, which would make the naming and the commissioning a single act.
suggested_refs: Gregory Nagy on Hesiodos as a speaking name
sources: Gregory Nagy, etymological reading as summarized in Hesiodic scholarship (not primary-verified in this pass)

stops.name: Ascra, the estate divided
stops.date_confidence: Undated. Works and Days 27-41 gives no year, no sum, and no names for the judges, and no independent record survives. Tradition rather than established event: the historicity of Perses and of the dispute is unresolved, with three live scholarly readings, real grievance, stylized memory, or pure didactic frame.
stops.campa: The father dies and the land is split. Hesiod says the division was already made when Perses seized the greater share and carried it off, swelling the glory of the bribe-swallowing lords who let him. Whether Perses ever existed is unsettled: scholars read him as a real brother, as a stylized memory of one, and as the addressee a didactic poem has to have. The accusation is delivered in verse, in the second person. No court is named and no figure given.
suggested_refs: Works and Days 27-41, the inheritance quarrel and its three competing scholarly readings
sources: Hesiod, Works and Days 27-41 (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: Ascra, the lords who swallow bribes
stops.date_confidence: Undated; the year orders the segment. The quoted words are verbatim in the Evelyn-White text, which prints the block as lines 212-224; the sentence itself falls at roughly 220-224. No local ruler of Ascra or Thespiae is named anywhere in the poem or in any other source.
stops.campa: The local basileis hear the case, and hearing cases is how they eat. Hesiod calls them bribe-swallowers and turns the phrase into the moral engine of the poem. He never names one of them, and never says how they ruled in his own case. Against them he sets the furrow, the season, the granary, and the flat claim that work is what the immortals love. Justice in his telling is a girl dragged through the streets while the men who sold her count out what they were paid.
stops.quote: There is a noise when Justice is being dragged in the way where those who devour bribes and give sentence with crooked judgements, take her.
stops.quote_source: Hesiod, Works and Days ll. 220-224 (printed by Evelyn-White in the block ll. 212-224), trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348
suggested_refs: The bribe-devouring basileis of Works and Days, the earliest Greek picture of local justice for sale
sources: Hesiod, Works and Days 212-224 (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: Ascra, Perses addressed by name
stops.date_confidence: Undated; the year orders the segment. The address is verbatim in the text. Whether the addressee is a living brother is the same unresolved question flagged at the inheritance stop.
stops.campa: The poem opens by splitting Strife in two. One breeds war and the wrangle at law; the other sets a man to work when he sees his neighbour's farm doing better than his own. Perses is told to take the second, stop loitering at the court-house to watch other men's quarrels, and plough. A brother is being lectured in public, at length, in hexameter, on the subject of his own conduct with money and land, and the lecture is addressed to him by name over and over through eight hundred lines. Whether he listened is recorded nowhere.
stops.quote: Perses, lay up these things in your heart, and do not let that Strife who delights in mischief hold your heart back from work, while you peep and peer and listen to the wrangles of the court-house.
stops.quote_source: Hesiod, Works and Days 25-29, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348
suggested_refs: The myth of the two Strifes, Works and Days 11-26
sources: Hesiod, Works and Days 25-29 (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: Ascra, the race of iron
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The Myth of the Ages is a mythic and rhetorical frame, not a datable description of conditions; it does, however, place the poem's own voice in a self-described era of broken kinship and broken oath. The year orders the segment.
stops.campa: Five races have lived on the earth and the man speaking belongs to the fifth. The golden lived under Cronos without grief; the silver was foolish and short-lived; the bronze destroyed itself; the heroes fought at Thebes and at Troy and were given islands at the edge of the world. His own is iron. In it kin turn on kin, oaths fail, the guest is robbed, and the man who swears falsely does well out of it. He says he wishes he had died before this race or been born after it.
stops.quote: First of all the deathless gods who dwell on Olympus made a golden race of mortal men who lived in the time of Cronos when he was reigning in heaven. And they lived like gods without sorrow of heart, remote and free from toil and grief.
stops.quote_source: Hesiod, Works and Days 109-113, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348
suggested_refs: The Myth of the Five Ages, Works and Days 109-201
sources: Hesiod, Works and Days 109-201 (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: Ascra, the year laid out by stars
stops.date_confidence: Undated; the year orders the segment. Flagged: the authenticity of the closing Days section has been questioned since antiquity and by modern criticism as a later addition, and this file does not decide it.
stops.campa: The work of the year is timed by the sky. Plough when the Pleiades set, reap when they rise, prune when Arcturus first shows at dusk, keep off the sea except for the fifty days after the solstice. Then the poem turns to the days of the month themselves and numbers them lucky and unlucky, the fourth for bringing a wife home, the fifth to be avoided because the Erinyes walk it. Ancient readers and modern editors alike have suspected this last section of belonging to another hand.
suggested_refs: The farmer's star calendar and the closing Days of Works and Days
sources: Hesiod, Works and Days, calendar and Days sections (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

segments.name: The Poems Made Under the Mountain

stops.name: Ascra, the Theogony begun
stops.date_confidence: Undated. Composition is understood as oral and performative development rather than a single act of publication; the year orders the segment. The Theogony is generally taken as the earlier of the two core poems, and its surviving text runs 1,022 lines, with the ending and some passages suspected of later interpolation.
stops.campa: He begins where the Muses told him to begin, with the Muses. The invocation asks for the holy race of the deathless gods, those born of Earth and starry Heaven and gloomy Night and the ones the briny Sea reared, and the poem then does exactly that for a thousand lines. It counts them, generation by generation, naming and placing every power in the world. Herodotus, centuries later, credits this poem and Homer's with giving the Greeks their gods' titles, offices, and shapes. The surviving text runs to 1,022 lines.
stops.quote: Hail, children of Zeus! Grant lovely song and celebrate the holy race of the deathless gods who are for ever, those that were born of Earth and starry Heaven and gloomy Night and them that briny Sea did rear.
stops.quote_source: Hesiod, Theogony 104-108, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348
suggested_refs: Herodotus 2.53 on Homer and Hesiod as the makers of the Greek theogony

stops.name: Ascra, Chaos and the birth of the abstractions
stops.date_confidence: Poem content, not chronology. The date orders the segment only; the material has no location in the world and no year.
stops.campa: First Chaos, then broad-breasted Earth, then Tartarus and Eros. Earth bears starry Heaven equal to herself, to cover her all about, and the hills, and the barren sea, and she bears them without any sweet union of love. A hill, a god, and a feeling enter the list by the same grammar; the poem is not sorting them into kinds. Night bears Doom and Death and Sleep, then Blame, Woe, the Fates, Nemesis, Deceit, Old Age, Strife, every one of them out of a body, every one with a mother named.
suggested_refs: Theogony 116-232, the first generations and the children of Night

stops.name: Ascra, Cronus and the stone in swaddling-clothes
stops.date_confidence: Poem content, not chronology; the date orders the segment. The succession sequence is textually secure in the Theogony.
stops.campa: Heaven hates his own children and pushes them back into Earth as fast as they are born, until Earth makes a sickle of grey adamant and the youngest, Cronus, takes it up. He cuts his father and throws what he cuts behind him into the sea, and out of the foam Aphrodite stands up. Then Cronus swallows his own children in turn, one after another as Rhea bears them, until she wraps a stone in swaddling-clothes and hands him that instead of Zeus. He swallows the stone.
suggested_refs: Theogony 154-210 and 453-506, the two overthrows

stops.name: Ascra, Zeus, the Titans, and Typhoeus
stops.date_confidence: Poem content, not chronology; the date orders the segment. Flagged as a modern interpretive frame rather than a biographical fact: scholars have compared this succession sequence to the Hittite-Hurrian Kumarbi cycle and to Enuma Elish, while recent work cautions against assuming direct literary borrowing and favours diffuse transmission over generations.
stops.campa: Zeus frees the hundred-handed ones from under the earth and they fight beside him ten years against the Titans, throwing three hundred rocks at a time until the sea boils and the earth cries out. The Titans go under Tartarus behind a wall of bronze. Then Earth bears Typhoeus, a hundred snake-heads speaking every voice there is, and Zeus burns him too. After that the poem stops narrating battles and starts allotting: honours and offices and portions, handed out god by god, until every power in the world has its share and the account can close.
suggested_refs: The Hittite-Hurrian Song of Emergence (Kumarbi cycle) and Enuma Elish, compared to the Theogony's succession myth
sources: Comparative Near Eastern scholarship following M. L. West, The East Face of Helicon (1997), not primary-verified in this pass

stops.name: Ascra, Prometheus and the woman made of earth
stops.date_confidence: Poem content, not chronology; the date orders the segment. The marriage maxims are textual fact about the poem and say nothing about Hesiod's own household: no wife and no child of his is documented anywhere in the tradition.
stops.campa: Prometheus cheats Zeus at the division of the ox and steals fire back inside a fennel stalk. Zeus answers with a woman. Hephaestus moulds her out of earth and water, Athena dresses and girdles her, Aphrodite pours grace over her head, Hermes puts in a shameless mind and lies. Out of this the poem takes its doctrine on marriage: take a virgin, it advises, so that a man can teach her careful ways. She lifts the lid of the jar, and what was inside goes out over the world. Only Hope stays under the rim.
suggested_refs: The Pandora narrative in both Theogony 535-616 and Works and Days 42-105
sources: Hesiod, Theogony 535-616 and Works and Days 42-105 (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

segments.name: Aulis to Chalcis, the Only Voyage

stops.name: Aulis, the one embarkation
stops.date_confidence: The event is attested in Hesiod's own voice at Works and Days 646-662 but carries no date. The conventional c. 700 BCE is a modern estimate resting on the disputed identification of Amphidamas; it is used here as a pin, not as a finding.
stops.campa: He has never been on a ship except once, and he says so before offering any sailing advice at all: he knows nothing of seafaring and nothing of ships. The one crossing he made was from Aulis, where the Achaeans once waited out the weather before Troy, over the strait to Euboea. The water at Aulis is narrow enough to see across. It is the only journey anywhere in the corpus told in the first person, and he tells it in order to disqualify himself as an authority on the sea.
suggested_refs: The strait of the Euripus at Aulis, crossed once and never again
sources: Hesiod, Works and Days 646-662 (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: Chalcis, the funeral games of Amphidamas
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the poet's own voice, undated. Amphidamas cannot be securely identified or dated. Flagged contradiction: the contest has been proposed at c. 730-705 BCE and connected to the Lelantine War between Chalcis and Eretria, while the war itself is conventionally placed c. 710-650 BCE, which widens rather than closes the circularity of the argument.
stops.campa: Amphidamas is dead and his sons hold funeral games for him, proclaiming the prizes. Hesiod crosses, competes, and wins a tripod with two handles. Who he beat, who judged, what category he entered and what he sang: none of it is in the poem. Amphidamas himself cannot be securely identified. Ancient and modern writers alike have tied him to the long war between Chalcis and Eretria over the Lelantine plain, and the dates of that war are themselves disputed.
stops.quote: Then I crossed over to Chalcis, to the games of wise Amphidamas where the sons of the great-hearted hero proclaimed and appointed prizes. And there I boast that I gained the victory with a song and carried off an handled tripod which I dedicated to the Muses of Helicon, in the place where they first set me in the way of clear song.
stops.quote_source: Hesiod, Works and Days 654-659, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348
suggested_refs: The funeral games of Amphidamas at Chalcis, the single datable candidate in Hesiod's adult life
sources: Hesiod, Works and Days 646-662 (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: The Valley of the Muses, the tripod dedicated
stops.date_confidence: The dedication is attested in Hesiod's own voice at Works and Days 656-659 and is undated. Coordinates approximate, as at the earlier sanctuary stop. What Pausanias was shown in the second century CE cannot be an authenticated eighth or seventh century object.
stops.campa: He carries the tripod back over the strait and inland and up to the ground where the goddesses first set him in the way of clear song, and leaves it there. The voice was given on this mountain; the first public proof that it worked comes back to the same hollow. Bronze, three legs, two handles, standing among the offerings of a rural sanctuary. Something claimed to be that tripod was still being shown to visitors here more than eight centuries later.
suggested_refs: Pausanias 9.30.1, on the tripod at Helicon said to be Hesiod's Chalcis prize, and 9.30.3, on the statues of the Muses and of Hesiod
sources: Hesiod, Works and Days 656-659 (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)
Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.30.1 and 9.30.3 (Jones, via Wikisource Book 9)

segments.name: The Oracle and the Roads West

stops.name: Delphi, the god names Nemea
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated. The oracle narrative survives in the Contest of Homer and Hesiod and in later lives; Thucydides 3.96, the earliest external notice, mentions an oracle that he should suffer death in Nemea but supplies no Delphic scene and no misunderstanding. Coordinates inherit the atlas pin for Delphi.
stops.campa: Delphi tells him he is honoured by the deathless Muses and that his renown will run as wide as the light of dawn, and then it names the place where he will die: the pleasant grove of Nemean Zeus. He takes this for the famous Nemea in the Peloponnese and keeps clear of it for the rest of his life. The oracle turns on a divine epithet, and the epithet belongs to more than one sanctuary in Greece. Thucydides, the earliest writer to mention the oracle at all, reports only that it foretold death in Nemea, and says nothing of Delphi or of any misunderstanding.
stops.quote: Blessed is this man who serves my house,--Hesiod, who is honoured by the deathless Muses: surely his renown shall be as wide as the light of dawn is spread. But beware of the pleasant grove of Nemean Zeus; for there death's end is destined to befall you.
stops.quote_source: The Contest of Homer and Hesiod, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348
suggested_refs: The Delphic oracle of the two Nemeas, in the Contest and in Tzetzes's Life of Hesiod
sources: The Contest of Homer and Hesiod (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)
Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 3.96 (Crawley, via Wikisource Book 3)

stops.name: Delphi, barred from the singing contest
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated, and unconfirmed at first hand. The claim rests on Pausanias 10.7.3 as characterized in secondary classical reference material; direct retrieval of that passage failed in this pass against Perseus, sacred-texts, and topostext.
stops.campa: A second Delphic tradition has him turned away from the Pythian singing contest on a technicality: he never learned to accompany himself, and the competition is for men who play. The Muses had given him a staff. A performer who cannot handle strings has no entry here, whatever the goddesses breathed into him on Helicon. Pausanias, reporting the story, notices the thing it turns on, that Hesiod's own verses put a laurel wand in his hand and no instrument at all.
suggested_refs: Pausanias 10.7.3 on the Pythian musical contest and Hesiod's exclusion
sources: Pausanias, Description of Greece 10.7.3, as characterized in standard classical reference material (primary text not retrieved in this pass)

stops.name: Nemea in the Argolid, the place avoided
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated, and negative: no source places Hesiod inside this valley. The stop marks the sanctuary the oracle was taken to mean. Wikipedia's article on Nemea does not mention Hesiod; the connection comes entirely through the oracle-pun tradition.
stops.campa: The valley in the Argolid where Zeus is worshipped, and where the games will later be held, is the one place the god's warning names. He keeps away from it, and nothing in any source puts him inside it at any point in his life. The whole legend depends on his believing this to be the only Nemea in Greece. A smaller and poorer sanctuary on the far side of the gulf carries the same divine title of Nemean Zeus, and nothing in the story suggests he has ever heard of it.
suggested_refs: The sanctuary of Zeus at Nemea in the Argolid, the famous Nemea of the oracle
sources: The Contest of Homer and Hesiod (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: Acarnania, where they claimed to have taught him divination
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated, and geographically unsupported: no itinerary or contemporaneous evidence places Hesiod in Acarnania, and no Acarnanian town is named in the surviving version. Coordinates mark the general region only. Reported via Pausanias as summarized in the research pool; the primary text was not fetched in this pass.
stops.campa: The Acarnanians of the western coast claimed him. Their tradition, reported by Pausanias, is that they taught him the art of divination, and poems on prophecy and on the meaning of birds circulated under his name for centuries afterwards. Works and Days already carries bird-omens and a long list of lucky and unlucky days, material enough for anyone who wants to build outward from it. No route brings him west in any source, and no town in Acarnania is named.
suggested_refs: The lost Hesiodic poems on divination and bird-omens, catalogued in antiquity
sources: Pausanias, as summarized in the research pool (primary text not fetched in this pass)

stops.name: Oenoe in western Locris, the long lodging
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated. The Oenoe stay appears in the Contest of Homer and Hesiod and in Tzetzes's Life. Coordinates are provisional: the exact site of Oenoe in Ozolian Locris could not be located to landmark precision in this pass.
stops.campa: He lodges at Oenoe in the western Locrian country, having crossed away from the Nemea he was warned about, and he stays a long time. The house belongs to men whom the sources name Ganyctor in one version and Phegeus in another, with sons whose names shift as well: Amphiphanes, Ganyctor, Ctimenus, Antiphus, depending on who is telling it. Where Oenoe stood cannot now be fixed on a map. The versions agree only that he arrived, and that he did not leave the district alive.
suggested_refs: Tzetzes, Life of Hesiod, and the Contest, for the Oenoe lodging
sources: The Contest of Homer and Hesiod (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)
Later biographical tradition as characterized in Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Hesiod', Death section

stops.name: The host's house, the accusation
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated, and internally contradictory. Plutarch's version explicitly exculpates him; other versions make him the seducer; the Contest names the seducer as a travelling companion called Demodes and says the girl afterwards hanged herself. One late strand makes her the mother of Stesichorus, which the conventional chronology will not carry. Thucydides, the earliest notice, mentions no sexual charge at all.
stops.campa: A fellow guest, a man of Miletus in Plutarch's telling, has secret relations with the host's daughter. The affair comes out and suspicion turns on Hesiod for having known about it from the beginning. Plutarch says flatly that he was in nowise guilty. Other versions make him the seducer himself. The Contest gives the deed to a travelling companion named Demodes, and adds that the girl afterwards hanged herself. Thucydides, writing closest to the event of any surviving author, mentions no woman at all.
stops.quote: A man from Miletus... had secret relations with the daughter of the man who entertained them; and when he was detected, Hesiod fell under suspicion of having known about the misconduct from the outset... although he was in nowise guilty
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Banquet of the Seven Sages 19, Loeb translation via penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: The sanctuary of Nemean Zeus, the oracle keeps its word
stops.date_confidence: The murder tradition at a named sanctuary of Nemean Zeus in Locris is attested by Thucydides 3.96, whose narrated events belong to Demosthenes' Aetolian campaign of 426 BCE. Culprit, motive, and circumstances are all later accretion and are tagged as tradition. The sanctuary's precise site is not settled by any landmark-precision source found here; coordinates are approximate for the Locris-Aetolia border zone.
stops.campa: The young men kill him in the precinct of Nemean Zeus and throw the body into the water that divides Achaea from Locris. Nothing in the earliest surviving notice supports either the motive or the disposal. Three centuries later an Athenian army under Demosthenes bivouacs in that same precinct on its way through the country, and Thucydides sets down what the local people say about the ground: that the poet Hesiod was killed here, an oracle having foretold that he should suffer this in Nemea.
stops.quote: He continued to stay a somewhat long time at Oenoe, until the young men, suspecting Hesiod of seducing their sister, killed him and cast his body into the sea which separates Achaea and Locris.
stops.quote_source: The Contest of Homer and Hesiod, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348
suggested_refs: Thucydides 3.96, the earliest surviving external testimony about Hesiod's death
sources: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 3.96 (Crawley, via Wikisource Book 3)
The Contest of Homer and Hesiod (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: The mouth of the Daphnus, the rock called Troilus
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated, and geographically inconsistent. A river Daphnus is elsewhere attested as an East Locrian, Opuntian toponym, while Plutarch's narrative otherwise places these events in the west near Molycreia and Rhium. The contradiction is recorded, not resolved; coordinates follow Plutarch's own narrative placement.
stops.campa: His servant Troilus goes into the water with him. The current of the river Daphnus takes the servant's body and lodges it on a rock that stands just clear of the waves, and Plutarch, writing something like eight centuries afterwards, says the rock is called Troilus to this day. A river of that name is attested on the eastern Locrian coast rather than the western one where the rest of the story is set. Nobody in antiquity reconciled the two coasts.
stops.quote: the body of Troilus, borne out into the current of the river Daphnus, was caught on a wave-washed rock... even to this day the rock is called Troilus
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Banquet of the Seven Sages 19, Loeb translation via penelope.uchicago.edu
suggested_refs: The rock named Troilus at the Daphnus mouth, still pointed out in Plutarch's day
sources: Plutarch, Banquet of the Seven Sages 19 (penelope.uchicago.edu)

stops.name: Rhium, the dolphins come in
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated. A recognizable Greek legendary motif, attached also to Arion; no physical or contemporary evidence supports it. Coordinates from Wikipedia, 'Rhium'.
stops.campa: A company of dolphins takes up the body as soon as it leaves the land, and carries it across the mouth of the gulf to Rhium, the narrows where the two shores nearly touch. The motif belongs to Arion of Methymna as well, and to half the drowned singers in Greek legend; no physical or contemporary evidence supports any version of it. What the dolphins do in the story is refuse the murderers their disposal of him. The body comes back to shore in daylight, on an inhabited coast, in front of people.
stops.quote: The body of Hesiod, as soon as it left the land, was taken up by a company of dolphins, who conveyed it to Rhium hard by Molycreia
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, Banquet of the Seven Sages 19, Loeb translation via penelope.uchicago.edu
suggested_refs: The dolphin-rescue motif shared with Arion of Methymna
sources: Plutarch, Banquet of the Seven Sages 19 (penelope.uchicago.edu)

stops.name: Molycreia, the body on the shore
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated. Flagged: the Wikipedia article on Molycreia does not itself mention Hesiod; the connection is drawn from Plutarch and from the Pausanias tradition reported in the research pool, not confirmed against that article.
stops.campa: The town nearest the landing is Molycreia, above the narrows. A local feast is in progress when the body comes ashore, and the crowd already gathered on the beach is the reason the killing is discovered at all rather than passing as a disappearance at sea. In Pausanias's version the sons of Ganyctor run from Naupactus toward this coast and are taken there. The Contest says the dolphins arrived during a feast of Ariadne. Molycreia's own surviving record says nothing about any of it, and no version agrees with any other on who was punished.
suggested_refs: Pausanias 9.31.6 on the flight and capture of the killers
sources: Plutarch, Banquet of the Seven Sages 19 (penelope.uchicago.edu)

stops.name: The Locrian coast, milk poured out with honey
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated, and Hellenistic in origin: a funerary epigram by Alcaeus of Messene, Greek Anthology 7.55, cited in the research pool's bibliography but not verified against the epigram's own text in this pass. Poetic commemoration, not an independent report of the death.
stops.campa: Nymphs wash the corpse where it lies and goatherds pour out milk mixed with honey over it. The lines belong to Alcaeus of Messene, a funerary epigram preserved in the Greek Anthology, written centuries after the events it commemorates and composed as a poem rather than as a report. No earlier writer mentions any of it. The men who tend goats on this coast do for the poet what nobody did for him while the body was in the water, and the nymphs of the place stand in for the household he never had.
suggested_refs: Alcaeus of Messene, funerary epigram for Hesiod, Greek Anthology 7.55
sources: Alcaeus of Messene, Greek Anthology 7.55, as cited in the research pool (not primary-verified in this pass)

stops.name: Naupactian territory, the first grave
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated. Flagged: the Wikipedia article on Naupactus contains no mention of Hesiod, his tomb, or a sanctuary of Nemean Zeus; the association rests on the Pausanias tradition reported in the research pool and was not verified against Pausanias's own text in this pass. Thucydides says he was buried at the precinct where he was killed, which is a different placement again.
stops.campa: He is buried where the sea gave him back, in Naupactian territory, and the grave is not marked in any way that the later searchers can find. Naupactus is a real town with a long recorded history and its own record says nothing about him. Everything that fastens Hesiod to this coast arrives through Pausanias and through Plutarch, both writing more than eight hundred years after the date conventionally given for the death. Thucydides, who is far closer to it, says he was buried at the sanctuary itself.
suggested_refs: The unmarked Locrian grave, and the conflict between the Thucydidean and Pausanian burial placements
sources: Pausanias 9.31.6 and 9.38, as cited in the research pool (not primary-verified in this pass)

stops.name: Ascra, one tower left standing
stops.date_confidence: Flagged as disputed. Wikipedia dates Ascra's destruction by Thespiae to 700-650 BCE, which sits awkwardly inside Hesiod's own conventional lifetime and is a bare assertion in that source; the single-tower observation is Pausanias's, in the second century CE. Wikipedia's stated distance of seven and a half miles contradicts its own coordinates, which give about 7.6 km, matching Strabo's forty stadia.
stops.campa: Thespiae puts the village down and the people scatter, and one account has them carrying Hesiod's ashes with them when they go. The distance between the two places is forty stadia, something under eight kilometres, an hour and a half on foot. Bad in winter, sultry in summer, good at no time: the line the poet wrote about his own village is the only description of it anybody kept. By the second century of the Roman empire a single tower is all that still stands on the site.
suggested_refs: The single surviving tower of Ascra, recorded by Pausanias in the second century CE
sources: Pausanias, Description of Greece, Boeotia, on the state of the site
Hesiod, Works and Days 639-640 (Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348)

stops.name: The rock cleft in Naupactian territory, the crow
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated. The date orders the segment only and carries no authority. The relic-recovery narrative comes through Pausanias 9.38 and Aristotle's lost Constitution of the Orchomenians, which survives only in quotation; no excavation has tested it.
stops.campa: Plague comes to Orchomenus and Delphi tells the city to fetch Hesiod's bones out of Naupactian territory. The searchers go, and they do not know where to look. A crow shows them, leading them to a cleft in the rock where the bones lie hidden. It is the standard machinery by which a Greek city acquires a relic it has no legal claim to: an oracle at one end, an animal guide at the other. Whether anything was ever carried out of Locris, no excavation has tested.
suggested_refs: Aristotle's lost Constitution of the Orchomenians, known only through later quotation
Pausanias 9.38 on the crow and the plague oracle
sources: Pausanias, Description of Greece 9.38, as cited in the research pool

stops.name: Orchomenus, laid by the tomb of Minyas
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, undated. Flagged: no source dates the Chersias epigram to a year; it is attributed to the seventh century BCE and Pausanias says the poem no longer survived in his own day. The date here orders the segment only. This burial conflicts irreconcilably with the Locrian death-and-burial tradition, and antiquity never resolved the conflict.
stops.campa: The bones come to Orchomenus in Boeotia and are laid in the ground there, in the agora beside the tomb of Minyas by the account that traces back to Aristotle's lost Constitution of the Orchomenians. The epitaph names both places at once, the village that made him and the city that holds him, and it concedes the first in order to claim the second. Chersias of Orchomenus is credited with the verses. Pausanias, who quotes them, says the poem they came from was no longer to be had in his own time, so the epitaph outlives the book it belonged to.
stops.quote: Ascra with its many cornfields was his native land; but in death the land of the horse-driving Minyans holds the bones of Hesiod, whose renown is greatest among men of all who are judged by the test of wit.
stops.quote_source: The Contest of Homer and Hesiod, trans. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Project Gutenberg ebook 348; a variant of the same epitaph is quoted by Pausanias 9.38.9-10
suggested_refs: The tomb of Hesiod in the Orchomenian agora, beside the tomb of Minyas
Chersias of Orchomenus, credited author of the epitaph

stops.name: Boeotia, the women in the catalogue
stops.date_confidence: Undated and disputed. The Catalogue of Women circulated as Hesiodic but is now generally regarded as later and composite; its date and authorship relative to the core poems remain debated. The year orders the segment only. Strabo's citation is verbatim from Geography 1.2.35, trans. H. L. Jones.
stops.campa: A long genealogical poem runs under his name, listing the mortal women who bore children to gods, and it is where the half-dog men, the long-headed men, and the Pygmies come from. Ancient and modern readers alike doubt that he wrote it. Seven centuries after him Strabo opens his Geography by defending Homer's monsters as deliberate invention, and sets Hesiod beside him in the same sentence: no one could charge Hesiod with ignorance when he speaks of men who are half-dog, of long-headed men and of Pygmies.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 1.2.35, defending Hesiod and Homer as deliberate mythmakers
The Catalogue of Women (Ehoiai), transmitted under Hesiod's name
sources: Strabo, Geography 1.2.35, trans. H. L. Jones (Loeb)

stops.name: Boeotia, the Shield and the poems that gather to a name
stops.date_confidence: Undated and disputed. The Shield of Heracles is generally dated from the end of the seventh to the middle of the sixth century BCE, so the year here is a placement within that range rather than a finding. Aristophanes of Byzantium suspected the Shield spurious and athetized the Precepts of Chiron (Quintilian 1.1.15); Athenaeus gave the Aegimius to Cercops of Miletus; Plutarch reported the Marriage of Ceyx as interpolated.
stops.campa: The Shield of Heracles, the Precepts of Chiron, the Marriage of Ceyx, the Aegimius: works carried under his name that ancient readers already doubted. Aristophanes of Byzantium struck at them; Athenaeus handed the Aegimius to Cercops of Miletus. Three lines of the Shield describe the Gorgon sisters who share a single eye between them, and in 1528 Giulio Camillo assigned that image to the fourth grade of his memory theatre at Venice, still crediting Hesiod for it two thousand years after the doubts began.
suggested_refs: Giulio Camillo's Theatro, fourth grade, emblematized by the Gorgon Sisters of Shield of Heracles l.230
Frances Yates, The Art of Memory, ch. VI
sources: Hugh G. Evelyn-White, introduction to the Loeb Hesiod (Project Gutenberg ebook 348)
